makingABudget.title: How to Make a Budget — With Tether-Zero and Your AI Coach in Your Corner

intro.p1: If you've ever reached the end of the month wondering where your paycheck went, you're not alone — and the fix is simpler than you might think. A budget is just a written plan for your money. It helps you make sure you have enough every month, keeps you from running out before the next paycheck, and gives you a way to save for goals and emergencies.
intro.p2: The steps below follow the classic budgeting process recommended by the Federal Trade Commission's consumer.gov. Along the way, we'll show how Tether-Zero handles the mechanics for you — and how Zero, your built-in AI coach, acts like a financial mentor who's already read your numbers and knows exactly where you are in the process.

whatIsABudget.heading: What Is a Budget?
whatIsABudget.p1: A budget is a plan that shows two things: how much money you make, and how you spend it. When you see those numbers side by side, patterns jump out — categories where you can spend less, areas where you'd rather spend more, and savings opportunities hiding in plain sight.
whatIsABudget.p2: Tether-Zero is built on a specific flavor of this idea called zero-based budgeting: every dollar you earn gets a job before the month begins. Your Budget board tracks this with the To Be Budgeted indicator — yellow when money is still unassigned, red if you've allocated more than you earn, and green when you hit exactly zero.
whatIsABudget.p3: New to zero-based budgeting? This is Zero's first job. Instead of sending you off to read tutorials, you can simply ask — “What does To Be Budgeted mean?” or “Why is my indicator red?” — and get an answer grounded in your budget, not a generic explainer. You can even pick the coaching style that keeps you motivated: the encouraging Cheerleader, the no-nonsense Drill Sergeant, or the data-driven Analyst.

gettingReady.heading: Getting Ready
gettingReady.p1: The traditional first step is gathering bills, pay stubs, and bank statements so you're working from real numbers instead of guesses.
gettingReady.p2: In Tether-Zero, this step mostly disappears. Connect your bank through Plaid sync and your accounts and transactions flow in automatically. Prefer to stay hands-on? Manual accounts, manual entry, and transaction import are fully supported too.
gettingReady.p3: Where Zero helps: With your transaction history connected, Zero can see your actual spending patterns from day one. Ask “What do I typically spend on groceries?” and you'll get an answer based on your real history — the honest starting numbers most first-time budgeters never have.

step1.heading: Step 1: List Your Bills and Expenses
step1.p1: Write down everything you spend money on: fixed bills like rent and utilities, plus variable expenses like groceries, gas, and entertainment.
step1.p2: In Tether-Zero, this list becomes your Category Groups and Categories — organize spending into groups like Needs, Wants, and Savings, with categories underneath. Sinking Funds handle irregular expenses (car repairs, holiday gifts, annual insurance) by rolling unspent balances forward month to month, and Smart Match auto-categorization learns your patterns and files incoming transactions for you.
step1.p3: Where Zero helps: Not sure how to structure your categories, or whether an expense belongs in a sinking fund? Ask. “Should my car insurance be a sinking fund or a regular category?” gets a practical answer with the reasoning behind it — the kind of judgment call that usually stalls new budgeters for a week.

step2.heading: Step 2: Figure Out Your Monthly Income
step2.p1: Total up what you bring in each month — paychecks plus anything else regular, like child support.
step2.p2: Tether-Zero gives income its own Income group at the top of your Budget board, with Planned and Received columns, so you can watch actual deposits fill in against your plan. If your income varies, the classic advice is to average your last twelve months — and with your history synced, that's a question Zero can answer for you rather than a spreadsheet exercise.
step2.p3: Where Zero helps: Zero also watches for income you didn't plan on. The Windfall Interceptor notices when a deposit lands well above your normal paycheck — a tax refund, a bonus — and prompts you before it quietly disappears into everyday spending: apply it to your top debt, and Zero tells you exactly how much interest you'd save and how many days sooner you'd be debt-free.

step3.heading: Step 3: Subtract Expenses From Income
step3.p1: Here's the core math: income minus bills and expenses. The result should be more than zero. If it's negative, you're spending more than you make.
step3.p2: The To Be Budgeted indicator computes this live as you allocate. And because zero-based budgeting asks you to assign every dollar, Tether-Zero flips the goal: deliberately allocate any surplus to savings or debt until you reach exactly zero.
step3.p3: Where Zero helps: This step is where budgets get emotionally hard — cutting back means choosing. Zero turns vague guilt into concrete trade-offs. Ask “Can I afford this $300 purchase?” and the Opportunity Cost Simulator answers with the actual consequence: “Technically yes, but it pushes your debt-free date back a week.” If you carry debt, Zero's Strategy Auditor goes further, watching your APRs and balances and telling you when switching between Debt Crusher's Snowball and Avalanche strategies would save you real money — with the Freedom Horizon chart showing the payoff date move as you decide.

step4.heading: Step 4: Use Your Budget Every Month
step4.intro: A budget isn't a document you make once — it's a monthly routine:
step4.li1: Beginning of the month: Make your plan. Copy Budget pulls last month's allocations forward in one click, and Zero can help you adjust it based on what actually happened last month.
step4.li2: Throughout the month: With Plaid sync and Smart Match, tracking mostly happens automatically — your job shrinks to a quick review.
step4.li3: Watch for problems early: This is where Zero earns its keep. Beyond the standard overspend alerts, Zero's predictive pacing alerts catch problems before they happen: if half your dining budget is gone by the 5th, Zero warns you that you're projected to run dry by mid-month and suggests a daily spend that gets you to the 31st. You course-correct on day 5, not day 31.
step4.li4: End of the month: The budget summary panel ranks your most overspent and underspent categories, and Zero can walk you through what the numbers mean for next month's plan.
step4.partner: Budgeting with a partner? Tether-Zero Households support shared budgets with role-based access — and Zero plays neutral third party. Instead of one partner accusing the other, Zero surfaces the data dispassionately: “Shopping is trending 20% higher than last month — want to look at the transactions together?” It also celebrates joint milestones, because crossing into positive net worth together deserves more than a spreadsheet cell turning green.

savings.heading: Make Savings Part of the Plan
savings.p1: The FTC's advice is to treat savings as one of your budgeted expenses rather than whatever happens to be left over — and zero-based budgeting bakes this in. Create financial goals in Tether-Zero with a target amount and date, and the app calculates the required monthly contribution and tracks your pacing. Ask Zero “How much do I need to set aside monthly to have $3,000 by June?” and you'll get the number plus a read on whether your current budget can absorb it.

finalThoughts.heading: Final Thoughts
finalThoughts.p1: Making a budget takes one sitting: list what you spend, total what you earn, and give every dollar a job. Keeping a budget takes a few minutes a day — less when bank sync, auto-categorization, and alerts do the bookkeeping.
finalThoughts.p2: What's historically been missing from budgeting apps is the coach: someone to answer “is this normal?”, “can I afford it?”, and “what should I do next?” in the moment, with your actual numbers in hand. That's Zero. It doesn't wait for you to dig through a help menu — it shows up contextually, right when a windfall lands, a category runs hot, or a strategy stops being optimal. The fundamentals of budgeting haven't changed since the FTC wrote them down. What's changed is that you no longer have to work them out alone.

meta.title: Your First Budget in 10 Minutes
meta.description: Tether-Zero's Smart Budget Customization Wizard turns five quick questions about your life into a personalized budget — no blank spreadsheet, no judgment.

intro.p1: The hardest part of budgeting isn't the math — it's the blank page. Most tools greet you with an empty spreadsheet or a wall of generic categories and wish you luck. So the first session becomes homework, and the budget quietly never happens.
intro.p2: Tether-Zero starts differently: with a short conversation. The Smart Budget Customization Wizard asks five quick questions about your life — the questions themselves take about a minute — and builds your budget around the answers. Add a few more minutes to give your first dollars a job, and you'll have a working budget in roughly the time it takes to brew a pot of coffee.

whyBudgetsFail.heading: Why most first budgets fail before they start
whyBudgetsFail.p1: Traditional budget templates drop you into about 35 ready-made categories, most of which have nothing to do with your life. If you don't own a car, why is there a category for oil changes? Before you've budgeted a single dollar, you're doing chores — deleting, renaming, second-guessing.
whyBudgetsFail.p2: There's a quieter problem too: entering your debts into a cold, clinical form can feel like being graded. Plenty of people abandon setup right there. Tether-Zero's wizard was designed to remove both failure points — it only creates what matches your answers, and it talks about debt the way a friend would.

fiveQuestions.heading: Five quick questions about your real life
fiveQuestions.p1: The wizard opens with “Let's build your budget” and asks you to name your household. Then it gets personal, in the best way: “Where do you live?” Renting, paying a mortgage, owned outright, or living with family — plus which utilities you pay. Each answer quietly becomes a budget category you would otherwise have created by hand.
fiveQuestions.p2: “How do you get around?” covers personal vehicle, public transit, rideshare, or bike and walking — with quick toggles for a car payment and car insurance. The wizard pays attention: mention a car payment here, and the debts step arrives with an auto loan already selected, marked “Added from your earlier answer — deselect if it doesn't apply.”
fiveQuestions.p3: The last question, “What do you spend on?”, captures lifestyle — streaming, dining out, the gym. Nothing feels mandatory: every step after housing has a “Skip this step” link, and if life interrupts you mid-setup, the wizard saves your progress and greets you next time with “Pick up where you left off?”

noJudgment.heading: The step with no judgment
noJudgment.p1: Between transportation and lifestyle comes the question most apps fumble: “What are you working to pay off?” The screen says the rest in Tether-Zero's own words: “This is what we're here to crush — no judgment.” Credit cards, student loans, personal loans, auto loans, medical debt — or simply “No debt.”
noJudgment.p2: The wording is deliberate. Debt in Tether-Zero is something you crush — it's the same spirit behind the Debt Crusher payoff planner — and crushing it starts here, by giving every debt payment a home in your budget from day one instead of treating it like a confession.

review.heading: Review everything, then “Create my budget”
review.p1: Nothing is created behind your back. The review step lays out exactly which budget groups and categories your answers produced, organized and expandable, so you can look before you commit. Something off? Step back, change an answer, and the preview updates. The budget only becomes real when you tap “Create my budget.”
review.p2: The result is typically a budget of 12–20 categories that actually match your life — not 35 you'll spend an evening pruning. A few essentials are always included, like Groceries and an Emergency Fund, and as the wizard itself puts it: “You can add, rename, or remove anything later.”

firstTenMinutes.heading: Your first ten minutes of actual budgeting
firstTenMinutes.p1: The wizard drops you straight into your new budget, and here's where the ten minutes earn their keep: giving your first dollars a job. Work down your categories in priority order — essentials first, then debt payments, then everything else — until the To Be Budgeted amount at the top reads $0. It turns green when you get there. That's zero-based budgeting: every dollar has an assignment.
firstTenMinutes.p2: If you run out of money before you run out of categories, that isn't failure — it's the most honest financial information you've had in a while. Fund what matters most; the rest waits for your next paycheck.

startingPoint.heading: A starting point, not a contract
startingPoint.p1: Your first budget is a draft, and that's the point. Over the next month you'll move money between categories, discover a bill you forgot, and fix estimates that were wrong — that's the budget getting accurate through use. Everything the wizard created can be added to, renamed, or removed. And the whole experience, down to your seeded category names, speaks English, French, and Spanish.
startingPoint.p2: When you're ready to go deeper on the method itself — the classic steps, and how Zero, your built-in AI coach, helps with each one — our guide on <link>how to make a budget</link> picks up right where the wizard leaves off.

meta.title: Give Every Dollar a Job
meta.description: Envelope budgeting, digitized: give every dollar a job with Tether-Zero's monthly allocations, sinking funds, and a To Be Budgeted number that tells the truth.

envelopeBudgeting.title: Give Every Dollar a Job: Envelope Budgeting with Monthly Allocations

intro.p1: Long before budgeting apps, people did this with cash and paper envelopes: payday came, the money got divided — rent in this envelope, groceries in that one — and when an envelope was empty, the spending stopped. It worked because it made one decision unavoidable: every dollar got a job before it got spent.
intro.p2: Tether-Zero is built on that same principle, minus the paper cuts. Each month you allocate your income across your budget categories until your income minus your allocations equals exactly zero — what the app calls balance to zero. This guide walks through how monthly allocations work, and how the app handles the arithmetic, the remembering, and the honest-mirror part for you.

envelopeMethod.heading: The envelope method, minus the envelopes
envelopeMethod.p1: In Tether-Zero, your categories are the envelopes. Every category row in your budget shows two numbers: Allocated — what you put in the envelope this month — and Available — what's still in it after spending. Fill them at the start of the month or whenever you're paid, spend against them, and glance at Available before any purchase you're unsure about.
envelopeMethod.p2: The Available number does the bookkeeping a paper envelope did physically: it's whatever you allocated, plus anything carried in from before, minus what you've spent. When it's healthy, spend without guilt. When it's low, that's the envelope telling you it's nearly empty — not a judgment, just arithmetic.

tbb.heading: To Be Budgeted: the number that tells the truth
tbb.p1: Above your categories sits To Be Budgeted — the money you have that hasn't been given a job yet. In the app's own words: “Green means you've hit balance to zero, yellow means money is still waiting, and red means you have assigned more than you have.”
tbb.p2: A positive number is unemployed dollars — money without a job tends to get spent by accident, so assign it, even if its job is simply next month's bills. A negative number means you've promised money you don't have; pull back from your lowest-priority categories until you're at zero. And zero is a floor for honesty, not a ceiling for savings — giving every dollar a job includes the dollars headed for goals and savings.

guidedSetup.heading: Let Guided Setup do the math
guidedSetup.p1: Facing a fresh month and a column of empty envelopes, you'll see a banner offering help with that month's budget: “Set each category one at a time — income first, with the math done for you.” Tap Start Guided Setup and the wizard does exactly that.
guidedSetup.p2: Its opening screen is titled, fittingly, Balance to Zero. Every answer saves immediately, so you can stop at any point and pick up right where you left off — and the To Be Budgeted chip updates as you go, so you watch yourself budget your way from yellow to green.

sinkingFunds.heading: Envelopes that remember: sinking funds
sinkingFunds.p1: Some expenses don't arrive monthly — car repairs, holiday gifts, annual insurance premiums. For those, mark a category as a Sinking Fund: unspent funds automatically roll over to the next month instead of resetting, so the envelope quietly grows until the bill shows up.
sinkingFunds.p2: Say your Car Repair fund carried $200 in from previous months and you allocate another $100 this month: Available shows $300, ready for the day the check-engine light wins. That's the difference between an emergency and an inconvenience.

newMonth.heading: A new month in one click
newMonth.p1: Once you've dialed in a month you like, you never start from scratch again: Copy Budget brings all of another month's allocations into the new one in a single click, and you adjust from there. Budgeting month two takes minutes, not an evening.
newMonth.p2: And when a category goes over — one will, and that's fine — Tether-Zero flags it plainly as overspent, you move money from a category that can spare it, and the month goes on. Do that consistently and the app even tracks your streak of consecutive weeks with no overspent categories. Overspending handled honestly isn't failure; it's the system working.

startSmall.heading: Start smaller than you think
startSmall.p1: The envelope method fails when there are too many envelopes. Ten categories you actually check beat forty you abandon — you can always split “Food” into “Groceries” and “Dining Out” later, once your real patterns show up. Your first month's allocations will be guesses; by month three they'll be facts.
startSmall.p2: And if you don't have categories yet, don't build them by hand: the Smart Budget Customization Wizard sets up <link>your first budget</link> around five quick questions about your life. Then come back here, give every dollar its job, and balance to zero.

sinkingFunds.title: Stop Getting Ambushed by “Surprise” Expenses: Sinking Funds Explained

intro.p1: Every budget has a villain story that goes the same way: the month was going fine, and then the car registration came due, or the vet found something, or December happened. The budget “blew up.” But look closer and most of these ambushes share a secret — they were never surprises at all. They were scheduled.
intro.p2: These are irregular certainties: expenses that don't arrive monthly but absolutely arrive. A sinking fund is the old, unglamorous, extremely effective fix — set aside a little every month so the money is already waiting when the bill lands. Tether-Zero builds them into the budget itself. Here's how to use them.

onSchedule.heading: Surprises that arrive on schedule
onSchedule.p1: Car registration comes once a year, every year. Tires wear out every few years, reliably. December brings gifts every single time. None of this is an emergency — yet these irregular certainties wreck more budgets than any restaurant habit ever did, because a monthly budget quietly assumes every month looks the same.
onSchedule.p2: It helps to keep two buckets straight. An emergency fund is for the genuinely unknown — the job loss, the broken arm. Sinking funds are for the known-but-irregular: you can name the expense, roughly when it's coming, and roughly what it costs. Different problems, different envelopes.

math.heading: The math that makes big bills small
math.p1: The trick is one division. Take a $600 insurance premium due in twelve months: that's a budget-breaking lump, or it's $50 a month and a non-event. Divide what the expense costs by the months until it arrives, and that's your monthly amount.
math.p2: Stack a few of these — $50 for the premium, $50 toward holiday gifts, $40 toward tires, $50 for a vet-visit buffer — and about $190 a month quietly disarms four future ambushes at once. The expenses didn't change; the schedule did.

flipSwitch.heading: Flip one switch in Tether-Zero
flipSwitch.p1: In Tether-Zero, a sinking fund is an ordinary budget category with one switch flipped. When you create or edit a category, enable Sinking Fund — the dialog explains it in one line: “Unspent funds will automatically roll over to next month.” Allocate to it like any other category, and on the 1st of each month the leftover balance carries forward automatically.
flipSwitch.p2: Set aside $100 a month for car insurance and don't touch it, and six months later the category shows $600 available. The fund's tooltip breaks the balance down — Allocated, Balance Forward, Spent, Available — so you always know how much is this month's money versus what's been quietly accumulating.

honest.heading: Honest even when you overspend
honest.p1: What if the bill arrives before the fund is ready? Say you've budgeted $200 for car repairs and the actual repair costs $230. The fund doesn't reset and pretend nothing happened — the $30 shortfall carries forward as a negative balance, so next month's $200 allocation shows $170 actually available.
honest.p2: That sounds strict, but it's the kindest thing a budget can do: show you the true number. A deficit that carries forward gets noticed and fixed with one extra allocation; a deficit that silently vanishes gets repeated.

fundOrGoal.heading: Sinking fund or goal?
fundOrGoal.p1: Tether-Zero also has Financial Goals, and the line between the two is worth knowing. A good rule of thumb: recurring cycles — insurance, holidays, car maintenance — work best as plain sinking funds. One-time targets with an amount and a date — a $2,000 vacation next August — shine as goals, which add a target amount, a pacing indicator that tells you whether you're on track, and progress visuals.
fundOrGoal.p2: If in doubt, start with the sinking fund. You can always create a goal later, once the thing you're saving for has a specific finish line.

spendIt.heading: Spend it — that's the point
spendIt.p1: When the expense finally arrives, spend from the fund like any other category. The balance drops — possibly to zero — and that's not a setback: it's the money doing exactly the job you hired it for, while the rest of your monthly budget never feels a thing. And if a fund outlives its purpose, Tether-Zero lets you release the category's available funds back to your budget.
spendIt.p2: Start smaller than you think: scan the last twelve months of statements for everything that made you say “where did that come from?”, then pick two or three funds — not ten. Fully funding car maintenance and holidays beats sprinkling $10 across eight envelopes. For how sinking funds fit into the bigger monthly rhythm, see our guide to <link>envelope budgeting with monthly allocations</link>.
